Neonatal Zebra finches emerge from eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] after a developmental period of 15 days [ab = 15 days], a duration that reflects the altricial nature of estrildid finches. At hatching, these altricial nestlings are nearly naked and exhibit a remarkably low wet weight of just 0.8 grams [Wwb = 0.8 grams], a mass that represents only a small fraction of the ultimate adult body size. This initial mass is consistent with the extreme altriciality of the species, requiring intensive biparental brooding and frequent provisioning during the first week of life. The rapid growth trajectory that follows is fueled by a diet of seeds and insects, with nestlings quickly depositing tissue and developing thermoregulatory capacity. The relatively short incubation period, coupled with the minimal hatchling mass, is an adaptive feature linked to the unpredictable rainfall patterns of the Australian arid zone, allowing for rapid breeding cycles following ephemeral resource pulses.

Fledging, defined as the moment the young bird attains the ability for sustained flight and leaves the nest, occurs at 17.5 days after hatching [tx = 17.5 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively brief nestling period is typical among small passerines and is likely an adaptation to reduce predation risk in open nest sites. Following fledging, juveniles begin a phase of wing muscle strengthening and foraging skill acquisition while still receiving occasional parental care. Subsequently, the onset of sexual maturity, or puberty, is reached at 60 days after hatching [tp = 60 days after hatching], marking the completion of gonadal development and the capacity for gamete production at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This parameter is measured in controlled aviary populations where food is abundant and social competition is minimized, allowing for a clear assessment of intrinsic developmental timing.

For the Zebra finch, the time since birth at first brood, representing the age at which a female lays her first clutch of eggs, is 300 days since birth [tR = 300 days since birth] when maintained at the species’ typical active metabolic temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This substantial delay between puberty and first reproduction, spanning roughly 240 days, is a period of high energetic demand as individuals navigate social hierarchies and acquire the experience necessary for successful parental care. Field observations of wild populations in central Australia often show even greater variation in this timing, as it is strongly influenced by the timing of rainfall and subsequent seed germination. The capacity to defer reproduction is a critical life-history strategy in a stochastic environment, allowing individuals to invest in survival until conditions are favorable for offspring rearing.

Once fully grown, the Zebra finch attains a maximum adult body mass, or ultimate wet weight, of approximately 11.7 grams [Wwi = approximately 11.7 grams]. This capacity for rapid population increase is a hallmark of an opportunistic breeding strategy.
